extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of poetry, philosophy, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and philosophical criteria for understanding and cultivating imagination, memory, and perception as they relate to poetry, philosophy, and literary creation. Emphasises mental faculties, conditions for association, and prudence in philosophical exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of the Imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination is an intermediate faculty which is at once both active and passive; in poetry we appropriate the name to a superior degree of the faculty, joined to a superior voluntary control over it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mind’s thinking process involves two powers relatively active and passive; the imagination is the intermediate faculty enabling these. The will can confine and intensify attention to give vividness to any object, showing distinction between ordinary association and poetic imagination. Example emblem: the water-insect that alternately resists and yields to a current illustrates the mind’s active/passive pulses in thinking and composing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts of Memory (qualities enabling sound passive remembrance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best, the only Arts of Memory are: sound logic; philosophical knowledge of facts under the relation of cause and effect; a cheerful and communicative temper; a quiet conscience; a condition free from anxieties; sound health; and above all (as far as relates to passive remembrance) a healthy digestion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artificial memory schemes are useless or absurd; true memory depends on moral, intellectual, and physical conditions. Cultivate temper, conscience, health, and disciplined thought rather than mnemonic tricks. These form the practical foundation for recollection and the imaging needed in creative production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conditions from causes (avoid paralogisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A common sophism is mistaking the conditions of a thing for its causes and essence; and the process by which we arrive at the knowledge of a faculty for the faculty itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-examine theories (e.g., Hartley’s) by separating contemporaneity/conditions from true causation. Example: the air I breathe is the condition of my life, not its cause. Failure to make this distinction yields paralogisms and category errors in philosophy and theory of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneity vs continuity in association and recall
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporaneity (co-presence in time) is a common condition of association, but whatever makes parts of a total impression more vivid or distinct will determine recall in preference to others equally linked by contemporaneity or continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must distinguish whether proximity in time or continuity in space occasioned association; vividness, likeness, and contrast (and the will’s intensifying attention) actually determine what is recalled. This is the practical general law of association relevant to composing and poetic imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: A theory of association does not explain perception
rubrics_metrics.description: None of the systems or any possible theory of association supplies or supersedes a theory of perception, or explains the formation of the associable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perception presents the object itself immediately to consciousness, not merely the product of associative inference or the transmitted effect of an external impact. Any adequate account of mind or art must address the immediacy of perception and the mechanism in the percipient that recreates the correspondent object, rather than reducing perception to chains of association or impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of materialism and hylozoism as explanatory frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Materialism (thinking as a property of matter) and hylozoism (life in matter) are inadequate to explain how affections from without metamorphose into perception or will; such systems either become unintelligible or collapse into spiritualizing matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid crude materialist or hylozoist reductions when accounting for mental phenomena in poetic or philosophical theory; these explanations either fail to account for the immediacy of the object in consciousness or require matter to be stripped of its material properties (becoming indistinguishable from spirit). Acknowledge the need for a mechanism in the percipient distinct from mere external impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites and prudence for Philosophy as a science
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy as an affectionate seeking after truth presupposes that Truth is correlative of Being and that intelligence and being are reciprocally each other's substrate; empirical doctrine alone (nihil in intellectu quod non prius in sensu) is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make philosophy scientific, one must accept certain postulates (e.g., antecedent conditions that render experience possible) and not resign intellect to mere observation and classification. Also practise prudence in exposition: where full answers would endanger the respondent or mislead readers, symbol or equivocation may be justified (as with Kant’s style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of heartfelt immediacy over polished orthography
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist writings on the human understanding and nature which would claim higher rank if they possessed as much fulness of heart and intellect as many simple pages of mystics (e.g., George Fox, Jacob Behmen); literati have often scorned such writers for lack of polished style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers and critics should bring superior spirit and judgment to discern value in simple, immediate expression; writers should not assume that polished orthography alone equates to depth. The simple, fervid expression of mystics can embody truths that learned style misses; avoid privileging form over genuine inspiration.
